transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, well, I came in because I keep getting stuck on this... this tiny uneven spot around my nose and cheek. It really bothers me when I see it in photos, or, you know, under the bright store lights where I work. And even when other people tell me they don't see it, it just... it feels like it's the first thing the customers and my managers notice when they look at me.
Do you find yourself checking mirrors, comparing your skin to others, or trying to cover up that spot multiple times a day?

Yeah, I do. Um, when I'm on my breaks at work, I usually end up in the bathroom just... checking my face in the mirror. I try to fix my hair around it to sort of hide it better. And I definitely catch myself comparing my skin to the girls who come through my checkout line. Sometimes I get so caught up looking in the mirror that I actually take too long, and... I end up being late getting back to the register.

When you're worried about how you look, is your main fear that this specific spot makes you look flawed or abnormal, or is it more that you're afraid people will judge or embarrass you in social situations in general, regardless of that spot?

Um, I think it's mostly just about that specific spot. I don't really worry about people judging me in general, or, like, just being around people. It's just... I feel like that one area makes my face look abnormal. I guess if I didn't have that uneven patch, I wouldn't really be stressed about talking to customers or anything. So it's definitely just about how that spot looks.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a preoccupation with a perceived minor flaw (uneven skin patch near nose/cheek) that is not noticeable or only slightly noticeable to others. This preoccupation is accompanied by repetitive behaviors (excessive mirror checking, camouflaging with hair, comparing her skin to others) that consume significant time and have caused functional impairment (being late returning to work). The fear is specifically tied to the perceived physical defect itself rather than general social judgment or embarrassment in social situations broadly, which argues against social anxiety disorder. There is no evidence of intrusive unwanted thoughts unrelated to appearance, compulsions outside of appearance-checking, or other criteria suggestive of OCD as a primary diagnosis. This clinical picture is consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22).
